svg.title: L/DMAX: best range and best glide speed
svg.desc: The L over D ratio is lift divided by drag. It reaches a maximum at one specific angle of attack and lift coefficient, where total drag in steady flight is at a minimum; any lower or higher angle reduces L over D and increases total drag. Weight and altitude do not change that angle or lift coefficient, but a change in weight alters the airspeed and power required to reach it. For headwind or tailwind there is no rule of thumb for maximum range. The best glide speed is published in the pilot operating handbook; in one PHAK case the published 110 knots did not reach the airport, and a lower speed would have given more thrust.
svg.text: L/DMAX: best range and best glide speed
The L/D ratio is lift divided by drag (CL divided by CD). The most lift for the least drag is obtained
at L/DMAX.
L/DMAX is one angle of attack
L/DMAX
L/D
Angle of attack (AOA)
Schematic of the L/D curve for a wing section
Steady flight at L/DMAX gives minimum total drag
Any AOA lower or higher reduces L/D and increases
total drag
For the PHAK example wing section, L/D reaches
its maximum at 6° AOA
What changes it, as PHAK states
Weight
L/DMAX occurs at a particular AOA and lift
coefficient, unaffected by weight or altitude
A variation in weight alters the airspeed and
power required to obtain L/DMAX
Headwind or tailwind
Many say speed up in a headwind or slow down in
a tailwind for max range; it is not always true
Each aircraft configuration is different, and
no rule of thumb covers all of them
Best glide speed
distance covered
The best glide speed is published in the POH
One PHAK case: a pilot with a failed propeller pitch
mechanism flew the published best glide speed, 110
knots, and could not reach the airport
The bulletin found that a speed below best glide
would have given more thrust to hold level flight
With variable pitch propellers, the speed to
maintain level flight may differ from the engine-out
best glide speed
